analysis.one_liner: Caps federal farm subsidy payments per person and closes loopholes that let big operations collect multiple checks.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee and died without a vote when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tightened the limits on how much federal farm subsidy money any one person can collect. It ended the "three-entity rule," which let one owner collect separate subsidy checks through several farms or partnerships, counted payments by real ownership shares so paper corporations could not hide them, required recipients to actually work on the farm rather than just manage it from afar, and cut the annual wool and mohair payment cap from $125,000 to $50,000. It also ordered a government audit of how the new limits worked.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund the farm subsidy programs, and smaller family-scale farms that compete against large operations collecting multiple payments through entities and partnerships.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the three-entity rule so a person with an interest in a third farming entity can no longer collect payments as a separate person, closing a widely used way to multiply subsidies [S2][S3].

Requires subsidy payments to corporations and partnerships to be attributed to natural persons in proportion to their ownership stakes, making it harder to stack payments through layered entities [S3].
Removes "active personal management" as a qualifying activity, so recipients must contribute active personal labor to be eligible — a change aimed at absentee owners [S3].
Cuts the annual wool or mohair payment limitation from $125,000 to $50,000 per person [S2][S3].
Directs the Comptroller General (GAO) to review implementation and report by name, state, and commodity any participants whose payments exceeded the limits [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large farming operations that used multiple entities, partnerships, or management-only status to collect more than the individual limit, and wool and mohair producers collecting payments above $50,000.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large subsidy recipients and wool/mohair producers

drawbacks.text: The biggest recipients of farm payments are often large, efficient operations; capping their payments could reduce their scale of participation and modestly affect production of supported commodities [S2].

Attributing payments through ownership shares and distinguishing active labor from management is administratively complex, which is why the bill itself builds in a two-year GAO review and report on whether the limits are enforced fairly [S3].
Wool and mohair producers whose income depended substantially on the program would see the per-person cap cut by more than half, a real income loss for high-volume producers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — closing loopholes that let a single owner collect several subsidy checks, and requiring recipients to actually work the land — flow to taxpayers and to smaller farms competing on a level field. The costs fall on a concentrated group of large operations and wool/mohair producers. The bill is tightly drawn and includes its own audit mechanism, so the main honest objection is administrative complexity and the risk that caps hit efficient large farms rather than abusive structures.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, the committee requested the Agriculture Department's views and then sat on it, and the bill died there without ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Penny of Minnesota and five cosponsors (4 Democrats, 1 Republican) introduced the bill on May 11, 1993 [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S5].
On December 10, 1993, the committee requested an executive comment from USDA — the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large farming operations that used the three-entity rule and multi-entity structures to collect multiple subsidy payments kept those arrangements intact, and wool and mohair producers kept the $125,000 cap. The House Agriculture Committee preserved control over farm payment policy, which never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large farm subsidy recipients and wool/mohair producers

for.name: Rep. Timothy J. Penny
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten farm program payment limitations and repeal the three-entity rule.

for.name: The bill's five cosponsors (Ms. Long, Mr. Leach, Mr. Minge, Mr. Pomeroy, Mr. Johnson of South Dakota)
for.role: Cosponsors in the House (4 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no further action recorded.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. E. 'Kika' de la Garza, D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, requested USDA comment, and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — Penny plus five cosponsors, 4 Democrats and 1 Republican.

industries.industry: Large farming operations and agribusiness entities receiving commodity program payments
industries.note: The bill ends the three-entity rule and attributes payments by ownership share, so operations that stacked payments through multiple entities, partnerships, or corporations would collect less federal money. Those payments come from taxpayers, so the industry's interest here runs against the public's.
The bill cuts the per-person annual payment cap under the National Wool Act from $125,000 to $50,000, cutting government support that these producers receive from federal funds.

industries.industry: Absentee owners and farm management entities
industries.note: By striking "active personal management" from eligibility, the bill requires hands-on labor for subsidy eligibility, ending payments to owners who manage farms without working them.
